newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU wrestles over beef aid and size of British cull.
newsitem.headline: EU wrestles over beef aid and size of British cull.

text.p: European Union farm ministers wrestled on Monday with proposals to help farmers and beef markets hit by new evidence that humans can develop a form of mad cow disease.

The evidence, announced by British scientists last week, strengthened the view of other EU countries that Britain must respect the bloc's Florence summit agreement in June on fighting the disease before any easing of a global ban on British beef.

"The Florence agreement has to be met. The accelerated cull has to go ahead," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, whose country now holds the rotating EU presidency, told reporters. German, Belgian and Spanish farm ministers agreed.

During a break in the meeting, British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg hinted Britain might drop some of its objections to the slaughter of extra cattle. "We certainly haven't ruled out a (selective) cull and a cull may take place," he said
Under the Florence accord, Britain should kill up to 147,000 extra cattle to try to stem the fatal cattle brain disease.
Hogg said Britain must first clear a backlog -- estimated at nearly 400,000 cattle -- to be destroyed under a separate scheme agreed earlier for animals over 30 months old.
He also said Britain would press for progress on exempting grass-fed herds which were free of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease from the ban on British beef exports.

Speaking again after private talks with EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, Hogg said, "We do want to make progress on the specialised herds. It may be necessary to have some kind of cull in order to get agreement with regard to those classes of herd."

A Commission spokesman said Fischler reiterated that the selective cull was a clear pre-condition for any lifting of the ban and it was up to London to decide whether to procede on a British or regional basis.

On the basis of current knowledge, Fischler felt that a regional approach using Northern Ireland would be more likely to receive support than other regions as its island location and computerised identifcation system made it easier to control BSE.
"Until we get a formal proposal from the U.K. we can't test the water on whether it would be acceptable to member states," the spokesman added.
But he emphasised that Fischler pointed out that in view of the ever-changing scientific situation it was impossible to prejudge reactions of member states.
Fischler emphasised an urgent need to agree a package of measures to reduce beef production in line with a drop in demand due to consumer fears that BSE could be passed on to humans.
But member states were deeply critical of plans to fund the 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) package, especially a scheme to slaughter new-born calves, by cutting aid to cereals farmers.
Fischler said cereal cuts were needed because 1.7 billion Ecus of unspent 1996 funds could not be transferred to 1997.
The Irish EU presidency plans to present a compromise paper when the ministers resume talks on Tuesday.
